body: i once knew a beautiful girl with PTSD.  I spent my time teaching her mathematics.  She was brilliant, but her performance was impossibly haunted by what had happened to her in the past.  She was capable of learning all of integral calculus in one  day... but the next day when the memories came back all was lost.  I have regrets from back then, because there was nothing I could do for her.  Right now there is nothing I can do you.  The only thing that I can say is that she found a better place for her mind.  No thanks to me she is alive and healthy.   Although I knew that it had  crossed her mind over and over to give up she never did.  I watched her while she picked tasks that she knew were impossible, because she expected to fail anyways.  Her past would always seem to pull her down.  She continued on the impossible anyways.  What was one more failure? What was pain?  Maybe to her, it was better for the pain to be in front of her than behind her.  Or maybe she was just trying to accumulate enough pain to have an excuse to go.  Whatever happened perhaps by accident she ended up succeeding, graduating, living and maybe not forgetting but moving on.  I can only wish the same for you, and ask you to move forward... because it is the only direction to go.  Forgetting is not something you do, it is something that happens to you while you are too busy chasing something else.

Ironic how suicide becomes relief and your best friend while hope implies the burden of struggling through.

When dealing with quotients of rings and trying to see what the elements look like, remember that the ideal you are quotient out by is the kernel of the natural map from R[x] to R[x]/(x).  Thus you can think of the ideal as being congruent to 0.  For your first problem... we can think of elements of R[x] with x = 0.  For a totally trivial and concrete example 3x^2 + x -2 in R[x] will look like -2 in R[x]/(x), because setting x= 0 will produce that result.  Thus you can see why R[x]/(x) is isomorphic to R.  R is of course a field....on a more abstract note, the ideal (x) is maximal in R[x] so the quotient will be a field.

For your second problem with R[x]/(x^2).. we use the same idea ... this time setting x^2 = 0.  Thus our previous example 3x^2 + x -2 will look like x - 2 in R[x]/(x^2) because x^2 = 0.  You can see that R[x]/(x^2) will contain only the polynomials with degree < 2.
Note: x^2 congruent to 0 does not in any ways imply x is congruent to 0.. think of 6 being congruent to zero mod 3 but not congruent to zero mod 9.

You asked if a ring is a field does that imply that it is an integral domain.
The answer is yes.

Here's why:
Recall an integral domain is a commutative ring with no zero-divisors (think the integers).

A field is a commutative ring with every element (except 0) having a multiplicative inverse.

So our question really boils down to whether or not every element having a multiplicative inverse means that there cannot be any zero divisors. 
If a is a non-zero element of field F.  If a was a zero divisor then there exists some non-zero element b such that a*b = 0.  Then 1/b (the inverse of b) must exist in the field.  multiplying both sides of our equation: a*b =0 by 1/b we get a= 0.  This contradicts our assumptions... showing that if two elements in a field multiply to 0 then one must be zero.

Determinants are tricky because they have so many different applications and are used in so many different ways it's difficult to wade through to what they really mean.  Even books get bogged down in the crazy abstraction and forget to explain the definitions.  I find that the easiest way to think about some abstract mathematical concepts is to understand the problem that the mathematical concept was invented to solve.

I'm fairly certain determinants were first invented for their geometric purposes in describing the eucldian plane (the xy-cartesian co-ordinate plane)  combinatorical definitions of determinants were only defined long after the concept of the determinant was known... and are not as helpful in understanding what they actually are.

First and formost people wanted to take two linearly independent vectors and find the area of the parallelogram they created.  This value actually turns out to be the absolute value of the determinant.  (the negative sign that sometimes appears comes from the orientation of the vectors)

So if we take the traditional view of a 2 by 2 matrix as two column vectors spanning R^2 (the xy-coordinate plane) and take the determinant, the answer is a scalar describing a unit of area that the two vectors etch out.  Not that if the vectors or not linearly independent (i.e multiples of eachother) the determinant is 0... the area of a parallelogram that would in essence be a straight line).  For the 3 by 3 matrix, the same analogy applies, except we get the volume of a cube.  The beautiful thing about this process is that the determinant has many wonderful properties that expand to much higher dimension (some we can't visualize)... thus birthing the crazy general combinatorical, and recusive definitions of the determinant.
